summary: For ages 7–9, teach fossilisation as an ordered CAUSAL chain with conditions: (1) an organism dies; (2) it is RAPIDLY BURIED in sediment (mud/sand) — the make-or-break step, because exposed remains rot or are scavenged; (3) soft parts decay while hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) remain; (4) over millions of years minerals carried by groundwater seep into the hard remains, filling tiny spaces and often gradually replacing the original material, while the sediment compacts and hardens into rock, preserving the shape; (5) later uplift and erosion expose it. Burial is necessary but does not guarantee a fossil. Make RARITY explicit so children reason that most living things leave no fossil, seeding the big idea that the fossil record is an incomplete, lucky sample. Use correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock, buried) in context. The strongest proposed activity is intended to let children choose settings, with quick burial decided by setting-dependent chance, and run time forward so that rarity may become an observed outcome rather than a stated fact; staged diagrams and ordering/check tasks support the sequence and vocabulary.
misconceptions: 'Fossils are the original bone, unchanged' — minerals usually replace the remains; a fossil is rock in the shape of the original.
'Any dead animal becomes a fossil' — fossilisation is rare; most decay or are eaten before burial.
'Fossils form quickly' — mineral replacement and rock formation take (typically) millions of years.
'Soft parts fossilise as easily as bones' — usually only hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) survive; soft tissue rarely preserves.
'Fossils form on the surface where the animal died' — burial in sediment (often water-laid) is essential; surface remains are lost.

activities.title: Play fate for a dead animal: vary conditions and run time forward
steps: For each of about 20 animals, choose where the body falls (e.g. muddy river delta, dry plain, open ground); the model then decides by chance whether sediment covers it quickly or it is left exposed. The odds depend on the setting: quick burial is more likely in a muddy delta and unlikely on dry open ground.
Advance a time dial forward through 'millions of years' and watch what happens for each choice.

For buried-quickly cases, observe the sequence: soft parts fade, hard parts (bone/teeth/shell) remain, minerals seep in and the bone colour-shifts to 'stone', sediment layers compact and harden into rock, then uplift and erosion reveal the fossil. Notice that some buried cases still end with no fossil (for example, the bone dissolves or the rock is later worn away), and some fossils are never exposed.
For left-exposed cases, observe scavengers and decay strip the body to nothing — 'no fossil'.
Keep a running tally of how many of the 20 animals became fossils, then state in your own words why fossils are rare.
Label each stage with the correct words: sediment, minerals, rock, buried.
activities.insight: Fossilisation is a conditional sequence in which rapid burial before decay is the crux. Burial is needed but not a guarantee, and because most animals are never buried fast enough, only a tiny lucky fraction fossilise, so the fossil record is incomplete.

activities.title: Compare buried vs exposed: the 'fossil or lost?' branch
steps: Look at two identical animals that die in the same place; one is buried quickly by sediment, the other is left on the surface.
Predict what will happen to each after a very long time, and say why.
Trace a branching diagram: buried quickly → hard parts remain → minerals replace them → rock → fossil; left exposed → rots/scavenged → no fossil.
Explain in one sentence why quick burial is the step that makes the difference.
activities.insight: Burial before decay is the pivotal condition that determines whether anything is preserved at all.

activities.title: Read the staged cross-section and label soft vs hard parts
steps: Study a staged cross-section: dead animal on a riverbed → layers of sediment pile on → minerals replace the bone → rock holding a fossil → erosion exposes it.
Reveal each stage's caption in order and retell the sequence aloud using the words sediment, minerals, and rock.
On a picture of an organism, label which parts are soft (usually lost) and which are hard — bone, teeth, shell — and typically survive.
Explain why we mostly find skeletons rather than whole animals.
activities.insight: The ordered sequence of fossilisation, and why hard parts are usually what we find because soft tissue rarely preserves.

activities.title: Order the stages and explain why burial matters (check)
steps: Put the stages in the correct order: dies → buried in sediment → minerals replace the remains → sediment hardens to rock → erosion exposes it.
Answer: why don't most animals that die become fossils?
Answer: what happens to the original hard parts over millions of years?

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.'
activities.insight: Consolidate and check the sequence, the role of rapid burial, mineral replacement, and the rarity of fossils.

checkQuestion: A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.
checkAnswer: Probably not. To become a fossil the body must be buried quickly in sediment before it rots or is eaten; then over millions of years minerals seep in and replace the remains while the sediment hardens into rock, keeping the shape. Left in the open it would decompose, so fossilisation is rare — most animals leave no fossil at all.
